response.description_long:
Platform teams merge dozens of times a day, and every one of those merges sits behind a pipeline that most engineers only ever see as a wall of raw log text. Pipewright's founding premise, stated plainly on its site, is that "the build is the least-observed system engineers touch every day. Application tracing got good; CI stayed a folder of log files." The company builds the missing telemetry layer for that system, aimed at platform engineering teams at companies between 20 and 2,000 engineers who need to cut CI spend and keep merge queues moving.

The product is a CI/CD observability platform for teams running builds on GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or Jenkins. A lightweight collector runs as a step inside the existing pipeline configuration — no agent daemons, no proxy — and streams timing, cache hits, artifact sizes, and test results to a backend where a columnar store keeps 13 months of history. Every pipeline run becomes a trace: jobs are spans, steps are child spans, tests are events, so the waterfall view familiar from application tracing applies to a build. The timeline is searchable by repository, branch, runner label, author, or a tag the user attaches in one line of configuration, and dashboards break duration down by repository, branch, and team.

The collector itself is a single static binary distributed for Linux and macOS runners, x86 and ARM. It reads metadata the CI system already emits — job names, step boundaries, exit codes, runner labels — and adds what the CI system does not report: cache hit ratios per restore key, artifact upload sizes and durations, and per-test timing parsed from JUnit, Jest, pytest, Go, and RSpec output. Everything is batched and compressed before upload, and the site claims a typical build adds 2 to 4 seconds of overhead, most of it parallel with teardown. If the backend is unreachable, the collector fails open, so builds never block on it. It needs no credentials beyond an ingest token and never sees source code.

Two features carry most of the differentiation. Flake detection replays a failing test in isolation on an ephemeral runner, up to three times, with the same commit and environment: consistent failure means a real break, inconsistent results mean a flake, which Pipewright then marks, tracks over time, and can file as a quarantine ticket in Jira or Linear. Cost attribution meters every job minute against the runner class that executed it and rolls spend up by repository, team, and pipeline, with budgets and alerts to catch runaway matrix builds before the invoice. The company notes that customers routinely find a handful of pipelines account for the majority of spend, and that half of that is cache misses. A third area, merge queue health, tracks queue depth, wait time, and eviction causes, distinguishing a slow required check from a flaky test evicting batches from runner starvation.

Pricing is published: a free tier for open-source projects and teams up to three developers with 90 days of history; Team at $30 per developer per month with 13 months of history, flake detection, cost attribution, merge queue analytics, and Slack/PagerDuty alerts; and Enterprise adding SSO, audit logs, self-hosted runner support, and a dedicated Slack channel on annual billing. Every paid plan starts with a 30-day trial and no credit card. Everything in the UI is available via GraphQL API, with a nightly Parquet export on paid plans and a Terraform provider for managing alert rules and budgets as code. The company cites SOC 2 Type II certification, per-tenant encryption keys, and a US data region; log payloads stay in the customer's CI system, with references stored rather than logs.

On traction, the site names Brightloop, Kestrelworks, and Fernrock Labs. Brightloop, a payments infrastructure company, took median merge-to-green time from 41 minutes to 14 after resharding its monorepo build on critical-path data. Kestrelworks, a game studio running 400-job nightly builds on self-hosted runners, uses cost attribution to bill CI back to game teams; its VP of engineering says the first week of data found a matrix build nobody owned burning a third of the runner fleet. Fernrock Labs quarantined 61 flaky tests in its first month and cut its merge queue's eviction rate by half. Pipewright positions against homegrown Grafana dashboards and scripts, arguing build telemetry is a product rather than a side project. The company was founded in 2022 in Seattle by Dana Whitfield and Arjun Mehta, ex-infrastructure engineers who ran build systems at a large e-commerce company, and is a 14-person remote-first team concentrated in North American time zones.
